name: Physics-Informed Learning
plain_language_definition: This whole series is about teaching computers to predict how physical things behave — how air pushes over a wing, how heat spreads through metal, how structures flex — by learning from examples instead of only writing down step-by-step math by hand. Physics-informed learning adds a new ingredient: as the computer learns, you also tell it the laws of physics you already know (conservation of energy, momentum, mass). The computer then finds a guess that both matches the examples AND obeys those laws.
ordinary_problem: A computer learning purely from data can accidentally find a guess that looks right on your measurements but breaks the laws of physics. This is especially bad when you only have a few examples, or when you need the guess to work for new situations the program has never seen before.
naive_picture: The simple hope is that if you gather enough examples of how a physical system behaves, a learning program can just memorize those patterns and act like a simulator — a program that steps a physical situation forward to predict what happens next — without needing to know the actual physics rules at all.
why_naive_fails: Real physics problems tangle together the governing equations (rules that say how things change moment to moment or place to place), the data you measured, how finely you divided space or time, whether small wobbles grow or shrink, and whether the answer makes sense scientifically. A learning program trained only on examples can look correct on your test data but fail when you change the setup slightly, run it for much longer, or ask it to obey a conservation law that was never written down in your examples.
first_principles: If you already know a physical law — the rule for how heat spreads, or how air pressure changes, or how energy must stay constant — then the computer should search only among guesses that respect that law. Instead of treating every data point as a separate instruction with no constraint, you add a penalty: if a guess breaks the physics rule even slightly, the learning program punishes it and tries something else. This way, the computer respects both the examples and the known laws at the same time.
what_breaks_without_it: Without this idea, you can build a learning program that scores well on examples you already have but falls apart when you ask it to predict something new — a different setup, a longer time, a pushed parameter. The program learned to copy patterns in the data without actually learning the deeper rule, so it has no way to generalize safely.
course_role: This topic ties together many of our seminars: it asks when and how you can combine learning from data with the math and laws you already know. It helps us ask the central question of this whole series — can learning programs predict physics faster and cheaper than hand-written rules, and when do they fail — more clearly.
worked_example:
Consider predicting temperature evolution u(x, t) in a 1-meter metal bar. The governing PDE is ∂u/∂t = α ∂²u/∂x² (the heat equation, with diffusivity α = 0.1 m²/s). You have temperature readings at the boundaries (u(0,t)=0°C, u(1,t)=100°C) and an initial condition (u(x,0)=50°C). A pure data model trained only on scattered measurements inside the bar would extrapolate poorly outside its training region.

Instead, a physics-informed neural network (PINN) penalizes both data misfit and the PDE residual: the network is trained to minimize L = λ_data · ||u(x_i,t_i) - y_i||² + λ_physics · ||∂u/∂t - α ∂²u/∂x²||² at collocation points. The second term is computed via automatic differentiation, enforcing the heat equation as a soft constraint. This allows the network to predict the smooth, slow diffusion that occurs deep inside the domain where no measurements exist.
deeper_mechanics:
A PINN represents the solution u(x,t) = f_θ(x,t) as a fully connected neural network with parameters θ. The composite loss function combines data fit and physics residual: L_total = L_data + λ_physics · L_residual, where L_residual = ||r(x,t)||² and r(x,t) is the PDE residual r = ∂u/∂t - N[u] (N[u] is the differential operator applied to u, e.g., α ∂²u/∂x² for heat).

During training, automatic differentiation computes ∂u/∂t and ∂²u/∂x² by backpropagating through the network definition. The gradient signal flows from the physics term directly: δL_residual/δθ = 2(r) · (∂r/∂θ), where ∂r/∂θ chains the residual through all parameter paths. This creates a coupled optimization landscape where the data and physics objectives compete; the weight λ_physics controls which wins locally.
failure_boundary:
PINNs fail when the PDE has sharp features (shocks, discontinuities) because the residual loss ||∂u/∂t - N[u]||² depends on second or higher derivatives; neural networks have weak spectral bias in high frequencies, so steep gradients amplify approximation error into the residual. For problems with long time horizons or extreme parameter ranges not seen in training data, the network's learned solution can drift outside the valid PDE regime (e.g., predicting negative density in fluid flow).

The stiff optimization landscape—where the data term pulls the network toward exact points and the physics term pushes toward the smooth manifold—can cause training to stall or oscillate. In inverse problems where parameters are unknown, adding a learnable parameter to the loss creates a highly ill-posed optimization with multiple local minima, and automatic differentiation through high-order derivatives becomes memory-intensive on large domains.

name: Reduced-Order Modeling
plain_language_definition: Reduced-order modeling is the idea that when you are simulating something physical—how air flows, how heat spreads, how a bridge bends—most of the interesting behavior happens in a small set of 'directions' or 'patterns'. Instead of tracking every single detail (which takes forever), you track only those key patterns. A neural network (a program with millions of dials that learns by trial and error) can learn to predict what those patterns will do next, far faster than running the full simulation.
ordinary_problem: Real simulations that predict physical behavior often need to solve thousands of equations at millions of points. Running these over and over—to test different designs, to find the best parameters, or to make decisions in real time—takes hours or days per run. In design, manufacturing, medicine, or robotics, waiting that long is not practical.
naive_picture: It looks simple: collect a bunch of simulation results as examples, throw them at a learning program, and then use that program instead of running the slow simulator. The learning program can answer instantly, and the problem is solved.
why_naive_fails: Simulation has hidden traps. The equations that describe physics have rules about conservation (energy, mass, momentum). The way you chop space into grid points affects what you see. Different starting conditions can lead to wildly different outcomes. A learning program trained only on surface agreement with examples will happily violate these hidden rules, and confidently give wrong answers when it sees conditions it has never encountered—different parameters, longer time, edge cases.
first_principles: the main idea is that most physical systems have natural structure. Their motion does not spread evenly across all possible states; instead, it travels mostly along a thin set of 'paths' or 'modes'. You can think of it like a video: it contains millions of pixels, but most of the action is carried by a handful of objects moving across the frame. If you recognize those objects and their trajectories, you can skip the pixel-by-pixel details. For physics, if you identify the dominant modes, you can build a much smaller model that predicts how those modes evolve—and that smaller model trains faster and behaves more like the real physics.
what_breaks_without_it: If you ignore this structure and just build a generic learning model, you end up with something that memorizes the training examples well but breaks as soon as the input drifts away from what it has seen: different material properties, longer simulations, rarer but important events. The model looks accurate in plots but fails in the real system, or in different scenarios, or when someone changes the problem slightly.
course_role: This seminar series asks: how can learning from data speed up or replace slow physics simulations? Reduced-order modeling is one answer: it finds and exploits the hidden structure in physical behavior so that a learning program can work on a small, fast model instead of a huge, slow one. This talk gives the ideas you need to recognize when and how this approach works.
worked_example: Suppose you want to simulate a rocket injector combustor: full 3D incompressible flow with combustion over 1 second. The spatially discretized Navier-Stokes equations yield 100 million unknowns. Running a single simulation costs 1 million CPU-hours; design optimization requires hundreds of runs. A reduced-order model (ROM) first collects snapshots u₁, u₂, ..., u_m by solving the full model at key time points. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) finds the dominant modes: a matrix V ∈ ℝ^(100M × 50) whose 50 columns span the 'intrinsic' subspace where the solution lives. The ROM approximates u ≈ V·a(t), where a(t) ∈ ℝ⁵⁰ is the low-dimensional state. A neural network predicts da/dt from the current modes, and running the ROM costs ~0.1 seconds. Trade-off: the ROM is 10,000× faster but only accurate when the new scenario stays within the training manifold.
deeper_mechanics: A ROM works by Galerkin projection: multiply the governing equation by V^T to project onto the span of basis vectors. If the full system is du/dt = f(u), then the ROM solves d/dt(V^T u) = V^T f(V a + u_ref), yielding k equations instead of n. POD extracts the basis V via singular value decomposition (SVD) of the snapshot matrix: [u₁ ... u_m] = U Σ V^T, and V retains the left singular vectors with σᵢ ≥ tol·σ₁. The challenge is that nonlinear terms in f(V a + u_ref) don't project cleanly—a term like u·∇u when restricted to the ROM becomes V^T (V a)·∇(V a), which is no longer a low-rank operation and requires additional closure modeling (like hyper-reduction via collateral POD or machine learning). The effective loss is ||du_ROM/dt - V^T f(V a)||² over training snapshots.
failure_boundary: ROMs become unreliable when the new scenario drifts outside the convex hull of training conditions. Parameter variation (different Reynolds number, boundary conditions, geometry), longer time horizons, or rare but catastrophic events (flow separation, transition to turbulence) can trigger responses that lie far from the POD subspace. Because the modes are passive—they encode history, not causality—a ROM trained on laminar flow may predict negative pressure or non-physical oscillations when subjected to transitional conditions. Instability grows exponentially in time: small projection error at t=0 compounds via the Lyapunov exponent, and the ROM solution diverges within 10–100 time units. Furthermore, nonlinear coupling terms are not accurately captured by the low-rank projection, leading to energy leakage and spurious damping or growth.

name: Differentiable Simulation
plain_language_definition: A way to run a simulator (a program that steps a physical situation forward in tiny increments to predict what happens next) and trace backwards through every choice it made, so you can see exactly how to tweak each input or design choice to get a better result. Like rewinding a video and nudging each decision along the way.
ordinary_problem: In science and engineering, you often don't just need to predict what happens given some input — you need to find what input would produce a desired result. For example: what shape of wing produces the most lift, or what sequence of moves makes a robot grasp an object most reliably.
naive_picture: A simpler idea: use examples of what a simulator does, feed them to a learning program (a network with millions of little dials it adjusts by trial and error until its answers match the examples), and let the network replace the simulator. Once you have enough examples, the thinking goes, the network should work just as well but much faster.
why_naive_fails: Real physical systems are tangled: equations describe behavior, but you also have measurement data, choices about how finely to divide space and time, uncertainties, and rules about what counts as physically sensible. A learning program trained only to match past examples can hide serious mistakes — it might look right on your training data but completely fail when you push it beyond what it has seen before, or when physical constraints get tested.
first_principles: A simulator is a chain of steps: inputs go in, the laws of physics get applied piece by piece, and outputs come out. If you keep track of how each step depends on the last, you can work backwards from the final result to see exactly how much each input influenced it. That backward trace tells you which direction to nudge each input to improve the result.
what_breaks_without_it: Without this tracing ability, you end up building models that perform well on test examples but warp and fail in ways that don't make physical sense when you try them on new conditions, over longer time horizons, or when you push the system beyond its training range. You can't steer the simulator toward better designs because you have no signal saying which direction to move.
course_role: This talk sits in the series about getting computers to learn physics from data instead of hand-written rules. Differentiable simulation is one of the main routes for doing that learning in a way that respects physical laws and scales to real engineering problems. Knowing this concept helps you understand why some learning approaches work and others hit walls.
worked_example: A wing design problem: given an airfoil shape parameterized by control points, you want to maximize lift-to-drag ratio at Mach 0.7. A differentiable simulator builds a forward model: shape → mesh → run CFD solver → extract forces. Each step (mesh generation, flux computation, time integration) is differentiable, so ∂(drag)/∂(shape) can be computed via reverse-mode AD, yielding gradients for all 50 design parameters in one backward pass. Classical optimization would require 50+ separate simulator runs (each costing 4 hours on HPC). Differentiable simulation computes gradients in 2× the forward cost. A gradient descent loop finds the improved geometry in ~10 iterations (40 hours versus 200+ hours). The key: the simulator is 'unrolled' as a computational graph, and backprop traces through all physics decisions.
deeper_mechanics: Differentiable simulation treats a time-stepping solver as a composition of differentiable operations: x_{n+1} = x_n + dt · f(x_n, θ), where θ are design parameters (shape, material properties). The loss L = Σ c_i(x_i) sums costs at each timestep or the final state. Backpropagation computes ∂L/∂θ by the chain rule: ∂L/∂θ = (∂L/∂x_final) · (∂x_N/∂x_{N-1}) · ... · (∂x_1/∂x_0) · (∂x_0/∂θ). Each Jacobian ∂x_i/∂x_{i-1} encodes the sensitivity of one step to the prior state, and all steps are 'unrolled' into a single computational graph. During backprop, every intermediate variable's gradient is stored (memory cost ~O(T) for T timesteps), or recomputed on-the-fly (checkpointing, memory O(√T)). The adjoint method gives the same result more efficiently for a single loss, avoiding explicit Jacobian storage.
failure_boundary: Differentiable simulation fails for ill-posed or chaotic systems: turbulent flows (Lyapunov exponent > 0) are sensitive to infinitesimal perturbations, so gradients computed through 100+ timesteps grow unboundedly or vanish, making descent directions unreliable. Discretization effects (time step size, flux limiter choice) introduce non-smoothness; a limiter that switches between schemes at a threshold discontinuously breaks differentiability. Shocks and sharp gradients demand careful treatment—standard finite-difference AD gives large errors when step size is too large or too small (condition number explosion). Long rollouts (> 10 Lyapunov times) make the gradient signal vanish exponentially in network-based surrogate models due to spectral bias. Also, the adjoint state must be integrated backward in time through all storage from the forward pass, demanding huge GPU memory; numerical drift in the backward integration can corrupt gradient accuracy even if the forward solve was accurate.

name: Operator Learning
plain_language_definition: Suppose you want to solve lots of slightly different physical problems — maybe heat spreading through bars of different shapes, or water flowing with different starting conditions. Instead of running a simulator each time, you train a program to learn the pattern: given one function (say, the starting temperature everywhere), spit out another function (the final temperature everywhere). That learned mapping between functions is an operator, and operator learning is the skill of training programs to capture these mappings fast.
ordinary_problem: In the real world, engineers don't solve one physics problem and move on. They solve families of related problems: the same differential equation (a rule that says how something changes from moment to moment or place to place) but with different starting conditions, different shapes, different material properties, or different boundary conditions (the fixed facts at the edges and at the start). Brute-force simulators have to run all the way through each time.
naive_picture: A first instinct: once you have enough examples of input-and-output pairs from a simulator, throw them at a neural network (a program with millions of little dials it tunes by trial and error until its answers look right), and it should learn to predict the next one instantly.
why_naive_fails: The real world is picky. A simulator balances multiple rules at once — the physics equations, the starting facts, the size of the tiny steps it takes, how errors accumulate, whether the math problem is stable or wiggly. A program that looks correct on the training examples might break when you move even slightly outside them: a new shape it never saw, a longer time window, a new boundary condition, or a scenario that violates physical rules in subtle ways. A bare neural network has no idea these rules exist.
first_principles: The right mental model: when you feed a function into the learned program and get a function out, you are not just predicting numbers — you are approximating an operator. An operator is a machine that takes one complete function (all the data, everywhere) and transforms it into another complete function. The program should learn to do this transformation in a way that respects the underlying physics, not just memorize examples.
what_breaks_without_it: If you skip this idea and just throw data at a black box neural network, you'll build something that works on your test set but crumbles in real use. It might predict fine for a familiar shape but fail for a new one. It might track the first few seconds right and then drift wildly. It might learn a pattern that looks like the physics but violates conservation laws or other hard rules that the real world enforces. Years of engineering then go to waste.
course_role: This seminar series focuses on training programs to predict how physical things behave by learning from data. Operator learning is one of the central routes for doing this when your problem involves solving physics rules for many different starting points or parameters. Understanding operators helps us ask the right questions: what should a program actually learn, and how do we make sure it still respects the laws of physics?
worked_example: The heat equation ∂u/∂t = ∂²u/∂x² must be solved for 100 different initial conditions (varying boundary conditions and domain shapes). A traditional solver costs 50 seconds per run (5000 seconds total). An operator learning model Θ learns the mapping: initial_condition(x) → final_solution(x, t=1). Training data consists of 1000 input-output pairs from the full solver. A neural operator (e.g., FNO—Fourier Neural Operator) applies convolution in Fourier space: v̂ = Θ(û) where û is the FFT of the input. One forward pass evaluates the learned operator on a new initial condition in 0.01 seconds, with 50 queries per second. The operator generalizes to different initial shapes, domain sizes, and final times if trained with sufficient diversity—inference is 100–1000× faster than the traditional solver.
deeper_mechanics: A neural operator learns G: A → U where A is the function space of inputs (initial conditions) and U is the function space of outputs (solutions). The Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) uses the spectral convolution: Θ(a) = σ(W_0(a) + F^{-1}(R(û) ⊙ F(a))), where F is the FFT, R is a learnable spectral filter (low-rank matrix in Fourier modes), and σ is a pointwise activation. Each layer acts on the Fourier representation, preserving translation invariance and allowing efficient computation. The loss is L = ||Θ(aᵢ) - uᵢ||₂² over training data pairs (aᵢ, uᵢ). Because convolution is scale-equivariant—scaling the input scales the output—the operator respects the homogeneity of the underlying PDE. Importantly, the operator is resolution-independent: train on a 128-point grid and evaluate on 256 points using FFT padding.
failure_boundary: Operator learning fails when the problem has strong nonlocal dependencies or strong nonlinearity beyond the training regime. A neural operator trained on smooth initial conditions may produce spurious oscillations or violate conservation laws (mass, energy) on new data. For PDEs with traveling shocks or steep fronts, the spectral representation has unbounded high-frequency content; the network's smooth basis functions (ReLU, Tanh) cannot resolve shocks, leading to Gibbs ringing artifacts. If the solution manifold has multiple branches (e.g., bifurcations in a dynamical system), the operator must output one deterministic prediction, but which branch is correct? Out-of-distribution parameters (different diffusivity, source term) push the network into unreliable extrapolation. Finally, long-time integration couples errors: rolling out the operator iteratively (u₁ = Θ(u₀), u₂ = Θ(u₁), ...) compounds errors exponentially, and the model diverges after ~100 steps.

name: Fluid Mechanics Simulation
plain_language_definition: Building a program that predicts how water, air, or any fluid will move and behave — where it flows, how fast, where swirls form, where shocks (sudden sharp changes) appear, and how the fluid's mass, momentum, and energy stay balanced as it moves.
ordinary_problem: Real fluids move in ways that are impossible to predict by hand — they change shape constantly, interact with themselves in intricate ways, create instabilities that spiral into chaos, and take enormous compute time to simulate step by step.
naive_picture: The naive hope: just feed a learning program (a computer's trial-and-error tuner of millions of dials) enough examples of fluid flows, and it will learn to predict the next moment without needing to run the slow step-by-step math.
why_naive_fails: Fluid flows involve tangled rules — how momentum shifts, how energy spreads, how the fluid piles up or thins out — that all talk to each other. The physical world also has hard constraints: mass can't vanish, energy can't jump around wrongly. A learning program trained only on examples learns statistical patterns, not the unbreakable rules. So it can produce answers that look right on paper but violate the physics, fail when conditions change even slightly, or blow up with wrong behavior after a few time steps.
first_principles: Any honest model of fluid flow must obey transport (stuff moves from place to place), conservation (the total amount of mass, momentum, energy stays the same or changes only in known ways), stability (small wiggle doesn't cause the whole system to collapse), and scale interactions (tiny eddies and large waves both matter and affect each other).
what_breaks_without_it: Without these rules baked in, you build a model that memorizes your training examples perfectly but fails the moment the fluid configuration is new, the time window is longer, or the boundary conditions (the fixed facts at the edges) change. It might predict negative density (impossible), violate momentum (breaking Newton), or suddenly flip behavior for no reason.
course_role: This theme anchors seminars about getting computers to predict fluid flows — either by teaching a learning program the physics rules alongside the data, by mixing a fast learned predictor with trusted physics math, or by learning in a way that guarantees the physics stays intact. It shows where the pure trial-and-error approach breaks and what precision and safety mean in this domain.
worked_example: Simulating incompressible flow past a cylinder at Re=100: solve ∇·u = 0 (mass conservation), ∂u/∂t + u·∇u = -∇p + ν∇²u (momentum balance, with kinematic viscosity ν=0.01). A traditional finite-volume method discretizes on a 2D mesh (100,000 cells), integrates forward dt=0.001 for 1000 steps (1 second simulated time), and costs 10 seconds per run. A data-driven surrogate trained on 500 pre-computed simulations (at varying Re, cylinder sizes) maps [u,v,p]ᵢ→[u,v,p]ᵢ₊₁. A pure neural network matches training data with low error but produces non-physical predictions: negative pressure, velocity magnitude growing unbounded, or mass accumulating in pockets. A hybrid model adds a correction term: [u,v,p]_corrected = solver_step([u,v,p]ᵢ) + neural_net_correction, ensuring conservation is preserved and the output stays within physical bounds.
deeper_mechanics: The incompressible Navier-Stokes residuals are R_momentum = ∂u/∂t + u·∇u + ∇p - ν∇²u and R_continuity = ∇·u. A physics-informed neural network penalizes both: L_physics = ||R_momentum||² + ||R_continuity||². For stability, the pressure term ∇p is often treated implicitly (pressure Poisson equation), which ensures the velocity field obeys the divergence-free constraint exactly. A hybrid approach uses the discrete divergence ∇·u computed via finite differences as a hard constraint: if the network predicts u_net, project it to the manifold of divergence-free fields via u_corrected = u_net - ∇(∆⁻¹ ∇·u_net) (Hodge decomposition in discrete form). The loss becomes L = ||u_corrected - u_true||² + λ·||div(u_corrected)||², ensuring both accuracy and continuity of mass.
failure_boundary: Fluid simulations fail catastrophically when the network learns non-conserving dynamics. Without explicit mass conservation, the predicted velocity field diverges (∇·u ≠ 0), and mass accumulates or leaks, distorting the pressure field and causing artificial vorticity amplification. In turbulent regimes (Re > 1000), the network must capture multi-scale eddies and their interactions; a small network misses dissipation at small scales, allowing unphysical energy growth. Shocks (discontinuities in density, pressure in compressible flow) are especially problematic: the network's smooth activation functions cannot represent sharp jumps, and the training loss smears them across multiple grid cells, violating the Rankine-Hugoniot jump conditions. Time-stepping accumulates error: a 1% per-step error compounds to about 2.7× after 100 steps ((1.01)^100 ≈ 2.7). For long rollouts (>1000 steps), compounding errors steer the solution far from physical manifold into negative density or superluminal speeds.

name: Hybrid Twins
plain_language_definition: A hybrid twin is a digital copy of a real physical thing—a machine, a structure, the weather—built by combining two approaches: a hand-written step-by-step math program (the simulator) that predicts what happens next, and a learning program (neural network: millions of little dials the computer tunes by trial and error until its answers match reality) that watches the real system and corrects the simulator's mistakes. Fresh data from the real thing feeds in constantly, so the digital copy stays in step with what is actually happening.
ordinary_problem: A pure simulator built from equations may miss forces or details that show up in the real world but were never written into the math. A pure data model—a learning program trained only on past examples—may give completely wrong answers once conditions change outside the range it saw during training.
naive_picture: You might think: once a learning program has seen enough examples, it can just replace the simulator entirely. Throw away the equations, let the neural network handle it.
why_naive_fails: Physical systems are tangled. They mix strict rules (conservation of energy), measured data (friction varies with temperature), numerical approximation tricks (how finely to chop space and time), hunts for steady states (does it settle or spiral?), and uncertainty about what we don't know yet. A learning program trained only to match past data will look good on those examples but will often break catastrophically when the real system meets new scenarios, extreme conditions, or corner cases—ways the system can behave that weren't in the training set.
first_principles: A good digital twin starts by using the equations for structure (they encode what never changes), adds a learning program for correction (to catch what we got wrong or left out), and pulls in new measurements constantly so it stays tuned to reality. The program learns not from scratch but by learning only the corrections, the things the pure equations miss.
what_breaks_without_it: Without combining these pieces, you build either a simulator that drifts away from reality, or a learner that works great on a test set but crashes when it meets something new. You lose the ability to trust your predictions, to know when something might go wrong, and to adapt when the real system changes.
course_role: This seminar series explores how to build and run systems that predict physical behavior. Hybrid twins are one important answer to the problem: how do you stay faithful to real physics while learning from data? This theme ties together talks about when to trust equations, when to trust data, and how to combine them.
worked_example: A robot arm in a manufacturing line is modeled by Lagrangian mechanics: M(q)·q̈ + C(q,q̇)·q̇ + G(q) = τ + τ_friction. Hand-written equations assume Coulomb friction τ_friction = -μ·sign(q̇), but real friction is temperature-dependent and varies with load. A physics-only model drifts 5° from actual arm position after 30 seconds. A data-only neural network trained on 1 hour of sensor logs (position, velocity, motor torque) fits perfectly but fails when the arm is loaded with a new payload. A hybrid twin solves: q̈_hybrid = M⁻¹[τ + τ_friction_learned - C(q,q̇)·q̇ - G(q)], where τ_friction_learned = neural_net(q̇, motor_current, temperature). The network learns only the error in friction (a low-dimensional correction), while the mass-and-gravity terms from physics provide the backbone. Training on just 10 minutes of new-payload data adapts the hybrid model, staying true while learning the unmodeled nonlinearities.
deeper_mechanics: A hybrid twin partitions the dynamics: x_{t+1} = f_physics(x_t, θ_known) + f_learned(x_t; θ_nn). The physics term encodes known structure (e.g., force balance, energy conservation); the learned term captures residuals: f_learned = network(x_t) ≈ f_true - f_physics. Training the network on residuals r_t = x_{t+1} - f_physics(x_t) is more stable than training on raw trajectories because the residuals are smaller and lower-variance. The loss is L = Σ ||x_{t+1} - f_physics(x_t) - f_learned(x_t)||². If the physics model is accurate, f_learned ≈ 0, and the network only needs a shallow architecture; this regularizes training. The update is performed as an ensemble: run the physics model forward, measure the actual outcome, compute the gap, and feed that gap to the neural network for online adaptation. Uncertainty quantification comes via Bayesian approximations (e.g., dropout) on f_learned, giving confidence bounds on the correction.
failure_boundary: Hybrid twins fail if the physics model is fundamentally wrong or missing dominant physics. If a heat transfer model assumes convection dominates but radiation is actually strong, no learned correction can recover the true dynamics consistently because the two effects have different temperature dependencies and spatial scales. The learned network becomes a band-aid that fits one regime but fails in another. If the physics model has unobserved state (e.g., internal temperature in a battery), the residual f_learned conflates multiple missing variables, and the network fits spurious correlations instead of true correction. Distribution shift—new operating conditions (higher load, new material properties) not in training data—causes the learned term to extrapolate unreliably. Time-accumulation errors also occur: a small error in f_physics compounds with small errors in f_learned, and over 100+ timesteps the drift grows exponentially. If the learned network is not kept simple relative to the physics backbone, it may exploit overfitting to residuals and violate conservation laws the physics model preserves (e.g., learning to violate energy conservation on transient events outside the training range).

name: Scientific Machine Learning
plain_language_definition: This series is about getting computers to predict how physical systems behave — how heat spreads, how structures bend, how air flows — by training a learning program on real measurements and simulation data, instead of (or alongside) hand-written equations. The program tunes millions of little dials by trial and error until its predictions match reality, then we use those predictions to run what-if scenarios, control the system, or fill in missing information.
ordinary_problem: Real-world science and engineering problems are stubborn: you have only a handful of expensive experimental measurements or runs (not millions of examples), you know some laws of physics that must hold, your simulators are slow and cost money to run, and making a bad prediction can lead to a broken airplane wing or a failed drug candidate — so guessing is not an option.
naive_picture: A naive hope is that once you collect enough data, a program trained on examples can just replace your entire simulator. Feed in the current conditions, read off the next state; done.
why_naive_fails: Physical systems are governed by equations that describe how things change moment by moment and place by place. A generic learning program knows nothing about these rules, symmetries, or the fundamental conservation laws (energy, momentum) that the real system must obey. It can memorize patterns in your data perfectly but still fail wildly on new starting conditions, longer time steps, or regimes you never trained on. It might predict that energy appears or disappears, that momentum is not conserved, or that stability breaks in ways the real physics forbids. A score showing 'accurate on test data' hides these failures until you run it on a real system and something breaks.
first_principles: Instead of letting the learning program invent its own rules, you design the learning problem around what you know: encode the physics equations and symmetries directly into how the program learns, inject uncertainty quantification so you know when to trust or distrust predictions, add the measurements you have as constraints, and structure the problem so the program learns to respect conservation laws and physical stability, not just match example data.
what_breaks_without_it: If you ignore this structure and just hand a generic learning program your data, you build a model that looks good on the examples you have but fails when: the system operates at a different scale or with different parameters; time horizons are longer than your training data; measurements are sparse or noisy; or real-world conditions differ slightly from your lab setup. The model breaks because it never learned to respect the underlying physics, only to copy patterns it saw.
course_role: This theme ties the whole seminar series together: every talk you will hear is exploring how and when learning from data can predict physical behavior when the exact rules are unknown or too expensive to compute. This one defines the core principle: marry what you know (the physics structure) with what you learn (the data patterns).
worked_example: Predicting protein folding energy given an amino-acid sequence and 3D coordinates: the energy is a sum of physics terms (electrostatic repulsion, hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic effect) plus unknown non-bonded interactions. Traditional all-atom molecular dynamics costs 100 hours per fold. Scientists collect 10,000 experimentally validated (sequence, structure, energy) triples. A pure neural network trained on these inputs predicts energy with 95% validation R², but when tested on a novel protein, it predicts an energy 100 kJ/mol below the true value, violating known bounds and suggesting the model learned non-physical artifacts. A scientific ML model embeds energy conservation: it outputs energy_nn + E_electrostatic(structure, charges) + E_vdw(structure, radii), where the second and third terms are hand-computed from known physics. The hybrid output respects bounds and reduces training error by 5× because the network only learns the remaining ~5% residual, not the 95% that physics already explains.
deeper_mechanics: Scientific machine learning adds physics structure to the loss function. Instead of L = ||y_true - f_nn(x)||², the loss becomes L = ||y_true - f_nn(x) - f_physics(x)||² or L = ||residual_data||² + λ_physics·||PDE_residual||² where PDE_residual = ∂u/∂t - N[u]. The loss is a multi-task objective: minimize data misfit AND minimize the residual of known conservation laws. For inference, uncertainty quantification via Bayesian approaches (e.g., Laplace approximation, ensemble methods) estimates confidence: q_uncertain = Var[f_nn(x) | data], allowing the practitioner to know when predictions are guesses. A critical trick is to use known symmetries as inductive biases: if energy should be translation-invariant, the network architecture is built to respect that (e.g., permutation-equivariant layers for molecular systems), so the symmetry is implicit rather than enforced by loss terms, which saves training data and improves generalization.
failure_boundary: Scientific ML fails when the practitioner encodes the wrong physics. If conservation of energy is imposed as a hard constraint but the true system dissipates (e.g., friction), the learned model will compensate by learning unphysical dissipation channels, and it diverges when dissipation changes. Sparse data—only 100 examples instead of 10,000—magnifies overfitting: the network learns noise correlations that masquerade as physics. When the true phenomenon involves rare events (e.g., a 1-in-1000-scenario phase transition), even 10,000 examples may miss it; the model confidently predicts the wrong behavior on that rare event because it has no signal to learn it. If the discretization (mesh size, timestep) affects the true dynamics but is not captured in the physics terms, the model fits one mesh scale perfectly but fails on another. Extrapolation beyond the training parameter regime is unreliable: a model trained on Reynolds numbers 100–1000 may hallucinate turbulence structure at Re=10,000. Domain adaptation is also fragile—a model trained on synthetic data (simulations) and applied to real data encounters distribution shift: unmodeled friction, sensor noise, or material heterogeneity that the synthetic data never saw.

name: Uncertainty And Robustness
plain_language_definition: Uncertainty and robustness ask: does a learned simulation model stay trustworthy when faced with gaps in the data it trained on, new conditions it never saw, tiny rounding errors that pile up, or running it forward for many steps in a row?
ordinary_problem: A surrogate model (a program trained to mimic a simulator) might get the average answer right but collapse exactly where decisions matter most—where scientists or engineers stake their conclusions.
naive_picture: The simple idea: once you feed a neural network enough training examples, it can just take over the job of a physics simulator. Collect data, train the network, and you are done.
why_naive_fails: Physics simulations involve many moving pieces: the equations themselves, the real measurements fed into training, the way you chop space and time into bits (discretization), whether the math stays stable over time, whether the model admits what it doesn't know, and whether the predictions actually hold up in a real experiment. A generic machine-learning scorecard (comparing guesses to examples) can look great while hiding failures that wreck the real system. The model might match training data perfectly but spiral into nonsense on a slightly different starting condition or after many timesteps.
first_principles: A robust model must do three things: tell you how confident it is (what it knows with certainty and what is a guess), stay stable when you nudge the inputs slightly or run it longer, and be checked in exactly the spots where mistakes would flip a real decision—not just on average, but at the edges where science or engineering judgment lives.
what_breaks_without_it: Skip this thinking and you end up with a model that plots beautifully against its training set but breaks the moment someone changes a parameter, runs the forecast much longer, or asks about a scientific quantity that depends on tiny details. The model becomes a false friend—looking reliable until it matters.
course_role: This theme ties together talks about knowing when a learned model is trustworthy, spotting where it fails, and building models that admit their own limits. It gives us a roadmap to decide which talks dig deeper into specific ideas.
worked_example: A climate model surrogate trained on 1000 IPCC climate scenarios predicts temperature anomaly ΔT in 2100 with 2°C mean error. When tested on a new scenario (1.5°C warming target), it predicts ΔT ≈ 2.8°C with high confidence (99%). But ensembles of the full climate model show ΔT ∈ [2.2, 4.1]°C (huge variance). The surrogate is overconfident: it saw similar patterns in training, so it extrapolates smoothly, but the true system's sensitivity to carbon-cycle feedback (tipping point) is new. A robust surrogate quantifies uncertainty: it outputs ΔT = 2.8°C ± 1.2°C (predicted std), flagging the new scenario as out-of-distribution and reducing confidence. During training, it was taught not just to fit (Σ_i (y_i - ŷ_i)²) but also to predict uncertainty variance σ_i² that matches residual magnitude (Σ_i [(y_i - ŷ_i)²/σ_i² + log σ_i²]) and to stay stable under small input perturbations (adversarial robustness).
deeper_mechanics: Uncertainty quantification embeds probabilistic reasoning into the surrogate. A Bayesian neural network outputs both mean μ(x) = f_θ(x) and variance σ²(x) via auxiliary network heads. The loss is the negative log-likelihood: L = Σ_i [(y_i - μ_i)²/σ_i² + log σ_i²], where the second term prevents the network from defaulting to high uncertainty to avoid penalty. Robustness to perturbation δx is measured via Lipschitz regularity: ||f(x+δx) - f(x)|| ≤ L·||δx||. This is enforced in the loss: L_robust = L_main + λ·max_{||δ||≤ε} ||f(x+δ) - f(x)||² or approximated via spectral normalization of network weights, which bounds gradient flow. For long rollouts, error accumulation is tracked: if one timestep has std σ_t, after T steps the bounds grow (optimistically) to √T·σ_t via random walk or (pessimistically) to T·σ_t via worst-case accumulation. The model flags when predicted variance exceeds tolerable bounds, signaling that the rollout is unreliable.
failure_boundary: Uncertainty estimates fail when data is sparse in high dimensions. A model trained on 1000 examples in 100-dimensional input space is severely underdetermined; its predicted uncertainties are likely miscalibrated (underestimates variance in the tail), leading to false confidence on truly novel inputs. Spectral bias in neural networks means the model learns low-frequency patterns first and high-frequency details late; uncertainty estimates may not account for residual high-frequency error that grows with time. In sequential prediction, uncertainty must be updated after each step, but neural networks are not truly Bayesian and don't properly account for prior information; the estimated posterior can drift from the true posterior, causing underestimated uncertainty that compounds over long rollouts. For systems with multiple stable states or bifurcations, the model's point estimate (mean) may predict state A with confidence, but the true system is in state B; the uncertainty estimate doesn't capture mode misidentification. If the training data contains systematic bias (e.g., all measurements from one instrument with a 5% calibration error), the model learns that bias and has artificially low residuals, so predicted uncertainty underestimates total error by a factor of 2–5. In adversarially robust training, the learned model becomes overly conservative and loses predictive accuracy on the clean distribution.

name: Inverse Problems And Control
plain_language_definition: Inverse problems are about working backward: you see what happened (the effect) and need to figure out what caused it (the hidden reason). Control is about picking actions now so that a physical system (a robot, a chemical reaction, a building in an earthquake) does what you want later. Both require a way to connect observations or goals back to the hidden causes or actions that produced them.
ordinary_problem: Every day, engineers and scientists face two recurring headaches. First: you measure something (a temperature reading, a video of water flowing, sensor data from a bridge) but you don't know what actually caused it—you have to work backward to guess. Second: you want a system to behave a certain way (a drone to hover steady, a chemical process to make the right product) and you have to figure out what to do to make it happen. Both need you to reverse-engineer the system or pick the right lever to pull.
naive_picture: The naive idea is simple: collect a bunch of examples of what happened, feed them to a learning program (millions of dials tuned by trial and error), and once it has seen enough, it can figure out backward causes or predict what actions to take—just like it learned a forward simulator.
why_naive_fails: Physical systems are not simple patterns. They hide real obstacles: the equations describing how things move are intricate and brittle, measurements are noisy, computers approximate things in chunks (called discretization), the slightest change to a parameter can blow up or crash your answer (stability), and science demands you respect real-world rules. A learning program trained on examples can look right on the test data but completely fail the moment you change a number in the equations, jump to longer timescales, or ask it to stay true to a known physical law.
first_principles: Here is the core idea: a forward simulator tells you what comes next—given a starting point and forces, it predicts motion. An inverse problem flips this around: given the motion you see, find the starting point or forces that explain it. Control does the same flip: given where you want to go, pick the forces or actions that get you there. Both rely on the forward simulator as the backbone but use it in reverse—either to search for causes or to plan for actions.
what_breaks_without_it: If you skip this idea and just treat the problem as 'fit a pattern to the data,' you build a model that memorizes the examples in front of you but shatters when you change conditions: different equations, longer runs, new parameter ranges, tougher constraints. You get a false sense of success until the model meets the real world.
course_role: This theme ties together seminar talks about working backward to find hidden causes and about choosing actions to steer systems. It anchors why a naive learning approach fails for these problems and where the real difficulties hide.
worked_example: In seismic imaging, geophysicists measure vibrations recorded by seismometers (the data) and want to infer subsurface rock properties (velocity c, density ρ). The forward problem: given the subsurface, the wave equation ∂²u/∂t² = c²∇²u predicts seismic waves. The inverse problem: given waves u_observed, find c and ρ. A naive approach trains a neural network: (seismic_record) → (velocity_field), fitting 100,000 synthetic examples. It predicts velocities quickly (0.1 sec) but misses sharp interfaces and violates the physics—the prediction doesn't satisfy the wave equation when checked. A physics-informed inverse solver uses differentiable simulation: iterate c_{n+1} = c_n - α·∂L/∂c, where L = ||u_simulated(c_n) - u_observed||² and the gradient is computed via adjoint wave equations. Five iterations (5 hours HPC) find c within 10% of truth, respecting wave physics exactly. Control is similar: given a drone with ∂x/∂t = v, ∂v/∂t = a + noise, choose thrusts a(t) to hover at (0,0). A learned controller maps (x,v) → a, but without physics it oscillates wildly. A control Lyapunov function ensures stability: design a(t) to minimize V(x,v) = x² + v² at each step.
deeper_mechanics: An inverse problem is formulated as: find m (model, e.g., subsurface properties) that minimizes misfit ||F(m) - d_obs||², where F is the forward operator (wave simulation) and d_obs is data. The gradient ∂misfit/∂m is computed via the adjoint: define λ as the adjoint state satisfying ∂²λ/∂t² = c² ∇²λ + (u_sim - u_obs), integrated backward in time. Then ∂misfit/∂m = ∫_0^T λ_t ∇²u dt (for velocity). This is an all-at-once gradient requiring only one backward solve, not 1000 forward solves (which naive differentiation would cost). For control, the optimal controller minimizes a cost J = ∫(x²+u²)dt subject to ẋ=f(x,u). The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation gives the optimal value function V(x,t), and u* = -∂V/∂x. A control Lyapunov function is V(x) chosen so that -∇V·f(x,u) ≤ -ρV (exponential decay), guaranteeing stability. Gradient descent in the parameter space of a neural network controller is the same as policy gradient for reinforcement learning.
failure_boundary: Inverse problems are ill-posed: many different models m can produce nearly the same observations F(m) ≈ d_obs due to noise, sparse measurements, or non-unique structure. A neural network inverts by memorizing correlations in training data; on test data with subtle differences, it guesses wrong. The adjoint gradient is accurate only if F is linear or if initialization is close to the true minimum; far from the solution, the gradient can point in completely wrong directions due to local minima (F is non-convex). Long time horizons in inverse problems compound this: if data spans 1000 seconds, the adjoint state is integrated 1000 times backward, and numerical error in the backward integration can corrupt gradients. For control, a naive neural network can find a policy that works in simulation but fails on a real robot due to unmodeled dynamics (friction, compliance); the controller is brittle to perturbations. If the true system is chaotic (e.g., climate modeling), no open-loop control can steer it reliably for long times—infinitesimal differences grow exponentially. If measurements are sparse or noisy, the inverse problem becomes even more non-unique, and the network learns one particular solution that is not robust to measurement error. Regularization (adding a penalty on model roughness) helps but can bias the solution toward overly smooth unphysical answers.
